problem: "It finds regression, not new defects" is self-contradictory: a regression is itself a defect newly introduced by a change. A student can read this as saying automated tests never report a bug.
fix: Automation re-runs known checks, so it mainly catches regressions (behaviour that used to work and now fails). It does not explore untested behaviour, so defects in new or unknown areas are still found by manual and exploratory testing.

where: Section 2, bullet list of pyramid layers
problem: The classic test pyramid has three layers: unit, service/API, UI. Listing "Behaviour layer: Cucumber scenarios" as a fourth layer implies BDD sits at one level of the pyramid, which is wrong; Cucumber scenarios can drive unit, API or UI tests.
fix: Drop the behaviour bullet from the layer list or say: "Behaviour-driven tests (Cucumber) are a way of writing the tests at any of these layers, not a separate layer."

problem: Section 3 lists run cost (machine time and people time to execute) as part of ROI, but the break-even formula R = B ÷ (M − A) contains no run-cost term. A student cannot see where run cost goes.
fix: State the assumption: "Here run cost is treated as small or equal for both options, so it cancels; if the automated run cost C per run is significant, use total automated cost per run A + C and R = B ÷ (M − A − C)."

problem: "The test plan from 5.1" and "the pipeline from 5.6 and 5.7" are bare numbers with no link, so a reader on a phone cannot jump to those chapters.
fix: Link each reference, for example the test plan from 5.1 and the pipeline in 5.6.

problem: "API checks and performance tests are strong candidates because they are fast and call little user interface" is awkward and unclear; "call" is not the right verb for a UI.
fix: "API checks and performance tests are strong candidates because they are fast and touch little or none of the user interface."

problem: "automation starts at 60 and rises by 2" gives 2 without a unit.
fix: "Automation starts at 60 person-hours (build cost) and rises by 2 person-hours per run."
